questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count pi electrons in cyclobutene opening
questions.stem: Working the problem, how many pi electrons are involved in the electrocyclic ring opening of cyclobutene?
questions.explanation: The ring opening converts one sigma bond into a pi bond while the existing pi bond reorganizes, involving four electrons in a 4n electrocyclic process that is conrotatory under thermal conditions.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Working the problem, the Cope rearrangement is denoted n,m where both indices are equal; what is the value of each index?
questions.explanation: The Cope rearrangement migrates a sigma bond across two allyl fragments and is designated a 3,3-sigmatropic shift because the bond moves from one end of a three-carbon allyl system to the other, so each index equals three.
questions.hint: Both fragments are three-carbon allyl units.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count electrons in a six-electron closure
questions.stem: Working the problem, a hexatriene electrocyclization involves six pi electrons. For which value of n does this fit the 4n plus 2 rule?
questions.explanation: Setting 4n plus 2 equal to six gives n equal to one, so a hexatriene is a 4n plus 2 system and undergoes disrotatory electrocyclization under thermal conditions.
questions.hint: 4n plus 2 equals six when n is one.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count atoms in the transition state
questions.stem: Working the problem, how many atoms are arranged in the cyclic transition state of a Claisen rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The Claisen rearrangement proceeds through a six-membered cyclic transition state involving the allyl group, the oxygen, and the aromatic ring carbons, which accounts for its high stereospecificity.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For the formula, in a Diels-Alder reaction, how many pi bonds from the diene and dienophile combined are converted into sigma bonds?
questions.explanation: Two pi bonds, one from the diene and one from the dienophile, are consumed to form two new sigma bonds, while the remaining diene pi bond becomes the double bond of the cyclohexene product.
questions.hint: Two pi bonds become two sigma bonds.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count atoms in the ring formed
questions.stem: For the formula, how many atoms form the ring in a Diels-Alder cycloaddition of a diene with a dienophile?
questions.explanation: Four atoms of the diene and two atoms of the dienophile combine to give a six-membered cyclohexene ring, which is why the reaction is a 4 plus 2 cycloaddition.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why is the endo Diels-Alder adduct usually the kinetic product?

answer.exemplar: In the endo transition state the electron-withdrawing substituents of the dienophile lie underneath the diene pi cloud, allowing favorable secondary orbital interactions between the pi systems that lower the activation energy; the exo transition state lacks these interactions, so although the exo adduct may be thermodynamically more stable, the endo product forms faster.

questions.explanation: Secondary orbital overlap lowers the endo barrier. In the endo transition state the electron-withdrawing substituents of the dienophile lie underneath the diene pi cloud, allowing favorable secondary orbital interactions between the pi systems that lower the activation energy; the exo transition state lacks these interactions, so although the exo adduct may be thermodynamically more stable, the endo product forms faster.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why do four-electron and six-electron electrocyclic reactions rotate differently?

answer.exemplar: The number of occupied pi orbitals determines the symmetry of the highest occupied molecular orbital, and the terminal lobes of that orbital have opposite phases for 4n systems but the same phase for 4n plus 2 systems; bonding overlap on closure therefore requires conrotation for 4n and disrotation for 4n plus 2 under thermal conditions.

questions.explanation: Orbital phase at the termini dictates the mode. The number of occupied pi orbitals determines the symmetry of the highest occupied molecular orbital, and the terminal lobes of that orbital have opposite phases for 4n systems but the same phase for 4n plus 2 systems; bonding overlap on closure therefore requires conrotation for 4n and disrotation for 4n plus 2 under thermal conditions.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why is the Diels-Alder reaction stereospecific?

answer.exemplar: Both new sigma bonds form simultaneously from the same face of the planar dienophile and diene in a single concerted step, so no bond can rotate before the product is formed and the original cis or trans relationships of substituents are preserved in the cyclohexene product.

questions.explanation: Concerted bond formation freezes geometry. Both new sigma bonds form simultaneously from the same face of the planar dienophile and diene in a single concerted step, so no bond can rotate before the product is formed and the original cis or trans relationships of substituents are preserved in the cyclohexene product.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why does an allyl phenyl ether rearrange to an ortho-allyl phenol?

answer.exemplar: The 3,3-sigmatropic rearrangement proceeds through a favorable six-membered transition state to give a cyclohexadienone that rapidly tautomerizes to the aromatic phenol; formation of the aromatic ring provides a strong thermodynamic driving force that makes the overall rearrangement favorable.

questions.explanation: Rearomatization drives the product forward. questions.explanation: Orbital phase at the termini dictates the mode. The number of occupied pi orbitals determines the symmetry of the highest occupied molecular orbital, and the terminal lobes of that orbital have opposite phases for 4n systems but the same phase for 4n plus 2 systems; bonding overlap on closure therefore requires conrotation for 4n and disrotation for 4n plus 2 under thermal conditions.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the chemistry: why is the Diels-Alder reaction stereospecific?

answer.exemplar: Both new sigma bonds form simultaneously from the same face of the planar dienophile and diene in a single concerted step, so no bond can rotate before the product is formed and the original cis or trans relationships of substituents are preserved in the cyclohexene product.

questions.explanation: Concerted bond formation freezes geometry. questions.stem: Explain the chemistry: why does an allyl phenyl ether rearrange to an ortho-allyl phenol?

answer.exemplar: The 3,3-sigmatropic rearrangement proceeds through a favorable six-membered transition state to give a cyclohexadienone that rapidly tautomerizes to the aromatic phenol; formation of the aromatic ring provides a strong thermodynamic driving force that makes the overall rearrangement favorable.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Discuss the reasoning: why is the endo Diels-Alder adduct usually the kinetic product?

answer.exemplar: In the endo transition state the electron-withdrawing substituents of the dienophile lie underneath the diene pi cloud, allowing favorable secondary orbital interactions between the pi systems that lower the activation energy; the exo transition state lacks these interactions, so although the exo adduct may be thermodynamically more stable, the endo product forms faster.

questions.explanation: Secondary orbital overlap lowers the endo barrier. questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Analyzing the data, why does HBr add anti-Markovnikov to an alkene in the presence of peroxides?

options.text: The reaction proceeds through the more stable carbon radical
The peroxide changes the alkene geometry
Bromine adds first as Br plus

questions.explanation: A bromine radical adds to the alkene so that the more stable carbon radical forms, and that radical then abstracts hydrogen from HBr; this radical chain gives anti-Markovnikov orientation unlike the ionic mechanism.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Based on the evidence, which ring size forms most readily in a radical cyclization?
questions.explanation: Five-membered rings form most readily in radical cyclizations because the transition state has favorable geometry and low strain, while smaller rings are strained and larger rings are entropically harder to close.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Based on the evidence, what is the typical geometry at a simple alkyl radical center?

options.misconception: that is typical of carbocations with sp hybridization

options.text: Square planar at the radical carbon

questions.explanation: A simple alkyl radical is approximately trigonal planar with the unpaired electron in a p orbital, so attack can occur from either face, which often erodes stereochemical information at that center.

questions.stem: In a practice exercise, which step in a radical chain generates the first radicals?

options.misconception: that is not a radical step

options.text: Homolytic cleavage of a weak bond by light or heat

questions.explanation: Initiation produces radicals by homolytic cleavage of a weak bond, such as a peroxide oxygen-oxygen bond, under light or heat; propagation then consumes and regenerates radicals and termination combines two radicals.

questions.stem: In a practice exercise, why does HBr add anti-Markovnikov to an alkene in the presence of peroxides?

options.text: The reaction proceeds through the more stable carbon radical
The peroxide changes the alkene geometry
Bromine adds first as Br plus

questions.explanation: A bromine radical adds to the alkene so that the more stable carbon radical forms, and that radical then abstracts hydrogen from HBr; this radical chain gives anti-Markovnikov orientation unlike the ionic mechanism.

questions.stem: In a practice exercise, which C-H bond is most reactive toward radical chlorination?

options.misconception: methyl is a type of primary
aryl C-H bonds are very strong

questions.explanation: Radical chlorination abstracts the hydrogen that leads to the most stable radical, so tertiary C-H bonds react faster than secondary, which react faster than primary, reflecting radical stability even though chlorine is not highly selective.

options.misconception: primary is less stable than benzylic

questions.stem: In a practice exercise, what role does tributyltin hydride play in radical reductions?

options.text: It initiates by forming oxygen radicals
It acts as a radical inhibitor
It donates a hydrogen atom to a carbon radical

questions.explanation: Tributyltin hydride transfers a hydrogen atom to a carbon radical in a propagation step, converting the radical into a reduced alkane while generating a tin radical that continues the chain.

questions.stem: In a practice exercise, what is the propagating species in free-radical polymerization of an alkene?

options.text: A carbon radical at the growing chain end
A carbocation at the chain end
A carbanion at the chain end

questions.explanation: In free-radical polymerization an initiator radical adds to a monomer to create a new carbon radical at the chain end, which adds successively to more monomer units in repeated propagation steps until termination occurs.
questions.hint: A chain-end carbon radical propagates growth.
